scenes.alt: Dario Amodei was so worried about Y2K that his high school teacher still remembers it decades later. He's been a doomer for much longer than I thought! While Shapiro taught a lot of smart kids over his 30 years at Lowell, there's ordinary smart and there's extremely, super bright kids, Shapiro said. Dario "was in that super bright category." But there was one anecdote about his former student that still puzzles the teacher. During the Y2K global panic over whether computers would work on Jan. 1, 2000 given a glitch in the calendar they used, Dario was "literally upset and worried about it." "I never understood. Yeah a lot of things will stop working for a few days, it will be a pain in the ass, but who cares?" he said of his own thinking. "I wasn't in the end of the world camp, and Dario was. FRANCIS FORD COPPOLA'S
MEGALOPOLIS
A FABLE

October 24th, 2026
Megalopolis Screening
Village East by Angelika

Dear Audience Member,
When a Motion Picture begins the audience enters through a door. But which door? Because just as fast-food companies spend millions making potato-chips habit-forming also movie companies spend millions making their 'products' as formulaic and addictive as they can. So when an audience is about to enter, they choose which door to open. Please choose mine: I've always wanted to make an Ancient Roman Epic set in Modern America; the parallels are so interesting. But my door is a new way in, not yet familiar and doesn't develop in ways you've been taught to expect. So please laugh when you want, shout out at it, be moved to tears or even if confused for a minute, you can still learn from it. Because when you're willing to open and enter a new door you may well reach somewhere you've never been before.

Thank you.
Sincerely
Francis Ford Coppola

MEGALOPOLIS Multi-Theatre Live Event
Village East Cinema 7 - New York, NY

Screenshot of a browser at rings.pondsiders.dev showing a 3D simulation of standing on the inside of a ring habitat. Flat green grass stretches to the horizon, with a large mottled gray boulder in the foreground. The ring’s surface curves up from the horizon into a pale blue sky and becomes an enormous band of land, water and cloud that rises straight overhead. Beside it hangs a gas giant striped lavender and peach, partly lit and partly hidden behind the band. Caption at bottom: “facing spinward · up 17.5°” and “24 mm lens, 53° tall · 33 of 75 minutes since midnight.”

A control panel on the left is titled “Installation 04,” with tabs Halo (selected), Orbital and Ringworld. Sliders read Time 10:31 AM, Year sun 24.0° stbd, Orbit Threshold 39%, Light +0.0 and Lens 24 mm, with a Play button set to 1 min / s. Toggles for Air (on) and REC sit beside the status “day · sun 58° up.” A Look section has buttons for Spinward, Antispinward, Up 45°, Port, Starboard, Zenith, Threshold, Basis and The sun. A Moments section offers Watch sunrise, Watch sunset, Behind Threshold, Full Threshold and The stars turn, followed by a “What am I looking at?” button.

A panel on the upper right, “Where you are,” shows a small diagram of the tilted ring around a pinkish planet labeled Threshold, a small moon labeled Basis, a “you” marker, and a bright sun labeled “Soell, far off.” Text below reads: “Not to scale. The ring rides round Threshold with its moon Basis, parked at the balance point between them, once every 3.7 days, and spins once every 75 minutes. Its axis is tipped 24°. Once a lap it passes through Threshold’s shadow for about three hours. Right now Threshold looks 39% lit from the ring. Drag to turn.”

Screenshot of a browser window at rings.pondsiders.dev showing “Installation 04,” an interactive 3D simulation of standing on a Halo ringworld. The scene is rendered from the ring’s surface: a flat green plain in the foreground, hazy blue sky, a sandy-textured band of the ring arching steeply upward on the left, a large banded gas giant (Threshold) in purple and tan hanging in the upper sky, and a grey cratered moon (Basis) rising near the bottom center. A caption reads “facing spinward · up 17.5°” with “24 mm lens, 53° tall · 33 of 75 minutes since midnight” beneath it.

A control panel on the left offers Halo, Orbital, and Ringworld modes; sliders for Time (10:31 AM), Year (sun 24.0° stbd), Orbit (Threshold 39%), Light, and Lens (24 mm); a Play button; and status text “day · sun 58° up.” Below are LOOK buttons (Spinward, Antispinward, Up 45°, Port, Starboard, Zenith, Threshold, Basis, The sun), MOMENTS buttons (Watch sunrise, Watch sunset, Behind Threshold, Full Threshold, The stars turn), and a highlighted “What am I looking at?” button.

At top right, a “Where you are” inset shows a small not-to-scale diagram of the ring between Threshold and Basis with the sun far off, plus a note that the ring orbits every 3.7 days, spins every 75 minutes, and Threshold currently looks 39% lit.

An open info dialog in the center explains the setting in three columns: the ring is based on Installation 04 from Bungie’s Halo: Combat Evolved, 10,000 km across and 318 km wide, parked at the Lagrange point between Threshold and Basis. It covers the two clocks (75-minute spin, 3.7-day orbit), how both worlds appear about 13° wide on opposite sides of the sky, eclipses lasting about three hours per orbit, and how the 100 km walls hide a low sun. It closes by noting which numbers were invented where canon is silent and that the scene is ray-traced per pixel.

Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment

    Open access
    Published: 09 November 2024

    Volume 182, pages 1813–1863 (2025)

In this paper, we characterize and challenge the preferentist approach, describing conceptual and technical alternatives that are ripe for further research. We first survey the limits of rational choice theory as a descriptive model, explaining how preferences fail to capture the thick semantic content of human values, and how utility representations neglect the possible incommensurability of those values. We then critique the normativity of expected utility theory (EUT) for humans and AI, drawing upon arguments showing how rational agents need not comply with EUT, while highlighting how EUT is silent on which preferences are normatively acceptable. Finally, we argue that these limitations motivate a reframing of the targets of Al alignment: Instead of alignment with the preferences of a human user, developer, or humanity-writ- large, Al systems should be aligned with normative standards appropriate to their social roles, such as the role of a general-purpose assistant. Furthermore, these standards should be negotiated and agreed upon by all relevant stakeholders. On this alternative conception of alignment, a multiplicity of AI systems will be able to serve diverse ends, aligned with normative standards that promote mutual benefit and limit harm despite our plural and divergent values.
